newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK inflation likely to thwart politicians.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK inflation likely to thwart politicians.

text.p: Election pledges on inflation from both of Britain's major political parties look set to be empty promises, according to a Reuters survey published on Monday.

A poll of 29 core inflation projections showed on average that expectations for retail price inflation in 1997 were 2.7 percent, while the mean of 28 RPIX forecasts for 1998 edged higher to 3.0 percent.

The predicted rates, although showing a high degree of stability over the next two years, miss the pledges from the ruling Conservatives and the opposition Labour party, both of whom have made medium-term promises ahead of the May 1 election of keeping RPIX inflation at 2.5 percent or less.
This measure strips out volatile and home loan costs. The Conservative party has promised to hit the 2.5 percent target by election day and keep it there for the duration of the next parliament.
Labour, well ahead in opinion polls, has promised to match or improve on that if it gains power.
But the predictions would probably be acceptable to policy makers during a long period of sustained, often vibrant, economic growth, analysts said.

They also reflect an increasing belief in a downward trend for British inflation -- RPIX predictions from Reuters surveys in January and last October both gave a mean forecast of 3.0 percent for end-1997.
The inflation forecasts from banks, research houses and academics were gathered as part of an exclusive quarterly poll of predictions for British economic indicators and exchange and interest rates.

"The domestic demand strength which you are seeing building now, this is to continue into 1998. The tightening labour market will be passed on next year as higher unit wage costs," said Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.

Latest available inflation figues show that RPIX fell to 2.7 percent in the year to February from 2.8 percent in January, but the Office of National Statistics warned that the downward trend may halt in March, when prices traditionally tend to rise.
Analysts said consumer spending figures and the payment of one-off bonuses by financial institutions as a result of stock market flotations would fuel inflationary pressure over the next few months.
Pressure from the Bank of England to raise interest rates curb fears of overheating, and a tightening in the labour market as jobless figures fall, were cited as danger signals for rising inflation.

The Reuters survey showed an average unemployment prediction from 25 forecasters of 5.5 percent by the end of this year, falling to 4.4 percent by the end of 1998 and 4.2 percent in the first quarter of 1999.
And although the manufacturing sector is currently suffering from the strength of sterling, the analysts said that the health of the services sector was also adding inflationary impetus.

"Sterling strength means that the manufacturing sector is still feeling the pinch in terms of export orders but the services sector is still very strong," said Alastair Bower, economist at Sanwa Bank in London.
The evidence from last week's purchasing managers' index highlights a soaring services sector and indicates there may be capacity constraints which will push up prices," he said.
